subject: physiology
title: Indicator Dilution, Inulin, Osmolarity, and Tonicity

steps.tx: Measuring the extracellular fluid volume requires a tracer that readily crosses the vascular capillary wall but cannot penetrate the plasma membrane of parenchymal cells. The uncharged fructose polysaccharide **inulin** fulfills these criteria precisely: after intravenous injection, inulin disperses rapidly throughout plasma and interstitial spaces while remaining excluded from the intracellular compartment.
steps.say: Inulin is the gold-standard tracer for measuring extracellular fluid. It crosses capillary walls into the interstitium but cannot penetrate cell membranes.

left.title: Inulin Properties
points: Inert uncharged plant polysaccharide
Freely filtered at the renal glomerulus
Neither reabsorbed nor secreted by tubules
Perfect tracer for ECF and glomerular filtration

right.title: Other ECF Tracers
points: Mannitol: inert sugar alcohol
Radiolabelled sulfate: distributes into ECF
Radiolabelled sodium: slightly overestimates ECF
Sodium enters cells in small amounts

steps.tx: To measure vascular plasma volume in isolation, the tracer must remain confined within the vascular lumen by the capillary endothelium. The synthetic azo dye **Evans blue** binds avidly to circulating plasma albumin with high affinity. Alternatively, radiolabelled serum albumin (131I-albumin) can be administered directly, enabling calculation of plasma volume from its circulating dilution.
steps.say: Plasma volume is measured with tracers that bind or match albumin, such as Evans blue dye or radio-iodinated albumin, which remain inside the capillaries.

steps.tx: Total blood volume is derived directly from plasma volume and venous haematocrit. Because whole blood comprises cellular elements and liquid plasma, total blood volume equals plasma volume divided by one minus the **haematocrit**. In an adult with a plasma volume of three litres and a haematocrit of forty percent, total circulating blood volume measures approximately five litres.
steps.say: Total blood volume is calculated by dividing plasma volume by one minus the haematocrit, typically yielding five litres in an adult.

steps.tx: Direct chemical determination of intracellular fluid volume is impossible because no tracer distributes into all cells without also equilibrating in the extracellular fluid. Consequently, intracellular fluid volume is calculated indirectly by subtracting extracellular volume from **total body water**. Deuterium oxide measures total body water, inulin measures extracellular volume, and the difference defines intracellular volume.
steps.say: Intracellular fluid volume cannot be measured directly. It is determined by subtracting inulin extracellular volume from deuterium total body water.

steps.tx: Solute concentration can be expressed in terms of weight or volume of solvent. Osmolality expresses the concentration of osmotically active particles per kilogram of solvent (water), whereas **osmolarity** defines particle count per litre of solution. In biological fluids with dilute aqueous solutions, normal plasma values range between two hundred and eighty and two hundred and ninety-five milliosmoles.
steps.say: Osmolality measures particles per kilogram of solvent, while osmolarity measures particles per litre of solution. Normal plasma values are 280 to 295 milliosmoles.

steps.tx: A critical distinction exists between total osmolarity and physiological **tonicity**. Tonicity refers strictly to the effective osmotic pressure exerted by impermeant solutes that cannot penetrate the cell membrane, such as sodium and glucose. Permeant solutes such as urea and ethanol cross cell membranes freely; they contribute to measured plasma osmolality but exert zero effective tonicity.
steps.say: Tonicity is the effective osmotic pressure created by impermeant solutes like sodium. Freely permeant solutes like urea increase osmolality without affecting tonicity.

steps.tx: Placing erythrocytes in solutions of varying tonicity demonstrates dramatic volume alterations. In a **hypotonic solution** such as 0.45% saline, the extracellular chemical potential of water is higher than the intracellular fluid, driving water into erythrocytes by osmosis. The cells swell, round into spherocytes, and undergo osmotic lysis if membrane mechanical tensile strength is exceeded.
steps.say: In a hypotonic solution, water moves into erythrocytes by osmosis, causing swelling and lysis. In a hypertonic solution, water exits and cells crenate.

left.title: Hypotonic Medium (< 280 mOsm/L)
points: Extracellular water activity exceeds intracellular
Net water influx into erythrocytes via aquaporins
Cellular swelling and loss of biconcave shape
Osmotic lysis and haemoglobin release

right.title: Hypertonic Medium (> 300 mOsm/L)
points: Intracellular water activity exceeds extracellular
Net water efflux from erythrocytes into medium
Cellular shrinkage and scalloped crenation
Intracellular dehydration and concentrated cytosol

steps.tx: Severe hypertonic states cause neuronal dehydration with life-threatening intracranial complications. Rapid elevation of serum sodium extracts water from brain parenchymal cells, causing brain shrinkage and traction tearing of delicate bridging cerebral veins. Conversely, treating chronic hypernatraemia with rapid plain water infusion causes sudden **cerebral oedema**, because accumulated intracellular organic idiogenic osmoles draw water rapidly into brain cells.
steps.say: Severe hypernatraemia draws water from brain cells, causing shrinkage and traction on bridging veins. Overly rapid correction causes cerebral oedema from trapped idiogenic osmoles.
